title: Instance-Based Learning
oneLiner: Predict by looking at the most similar past examples, and choose settings honestly with validation.

what.html:
Instance-based learning keeps the training examples and, when a new case arrives, finds the most similar stored cases and copies their answer. The best-known method is k-nearest neighbours (k-NN).

Everyday version"If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's probably a duck." To guess a house price, look up the five most similar houses that sold recently and average their prices.

There's no training step that builds a formula. These are lazy learners: fast to train, slower to predict. Model-based (eager) learners do the opposite.

why.html:
• No assumptions about shape. The boundary can be as wiggly as the data needs.
  • Adapts instantly. Add new examples and the predictions update; nothing to retrain.
  • Works for categories and numbers: vote for a class, or average a value.
  • The same "similarity" idea powers recommenders, search and clustering.

how.title: Store, then compare
how.html: Model-based: learn parameters θ, throw the data away, predict with f(x). Instance-based: keep all (x, y) pairs; when asked about a new x, search for similar stored points and use them.

how.title: Ask the k nearest neighbours
how.html: For a category: take a vote among the k closest points. For a number: take their mean (or median). The answer can change with k, as the slides' problem shows: with k = 3 or 5 the point (1, 1) is Positive, with k = 7 it becomes Negative.

how.title: What does 'near' mean? Distances
how.html: Euclidean: straight-line distance. Manhattan: city-block distance (walk along streets). Supremum: the single biggest difference along any one feature. All three belong to one family, the Minkowski distance, controlled by a number h (1, 2, ∞).

how.title: Distances for yes/no and category data
how.html: For categories, count mismatches: two people who differ in 2 of 4 attributes are 0.5 apart. For yes/no symptoms where "no" is common and uninformative (asymmetric), ignore the shared "no"s; the Jaccard idea. Among the slides' patients, Jack and Mary are most alike (0.33).

how.title: Put features on the same scale
how.html: If income is in tens of thousands and age is in years, income dominates every distance. Standardise (z-score) or min-max scale first; otherwise "nearest" really means "nearest in income".

how.title: Mixed data: Gower distance
how.html: Real tables mix numbers, categories and ranks. Gower distance scores each column between 0 and 1 in its own way (scaled difference for numbers and ranks, 0/1 mismatch for categories) and averages them. In the slides' example Balram and Bharat are the most similar pair.

how.title: Too many features ruin 'near'
how.html: With many irrelevant attributes, two truly similar cases can look far apart because random differences add up. This is the curse of dimensionality. Fix: weight the important features more, or drop the irrelevant ones (choose using cross-validation).

how.title: Choosing k
how.html: Small k follows every noisy point (overfits); large k blurs everything toward the majority (underfits). A rule of thumb is k ≈ √N. Better: plot the validation error for k = 1, 2, 3… and pick where the curve flattens (the elbow).

how.title: Let closer neighbours count more
how.html: Distance-weighted k-NN gives each neighbour a vote proportional to 1/distance². In the slides' customer example, plain voting picks L2, but weighted voting picks L1, because the two L1 customers are much closer.

how.title: Fit a little model around each question
how.html: Locally weighted regression fits a fresh straight line for every query, using only nearby points and trusting the closest ones most (a bell-shaped kernel). The result follows curves that a single global line can't.

how.title: Strengths and costs
how.html: Great for low-dimensional data, lots of training data, complex targets, and it smooths noise when weighted. But every prediction compares against all stored points (slow), all data must be kept (memory), and you must pick k and the distance. Speed-ups: kd-trees and removing redundant points.

how.title: Honest evaluation: train, validate, test
how.html: Never tune on the test set: if you try 100 settings and keep the one that looks best on the test set, that score is a lucky fluke. Tune on a validation set, or better, use k-fold cross-validation: rotate which fold is held out and average. Touch the test set once, at the very end.

demo.html: The slides' 13 labelled points (white and pink). Drag the black query point, change k, and switch on distance weighting. Circles show the neighbours that vote; the background shows what k-NN would predict everywhere. Try k = 1 (jagged islands) and k = 13 (everything becomes the majority).

example.html:
House prices. To price a 2,000 sq ft house, 3-NN averages the three most similar sales: (50 + 55 + 51)/3 = 52 (in the slides' units).

Customer type. A bank classifies a new customer (income, profession, region, locality) by finding the most similar existing customers with a Gower-style distance.

Supplementary In telecom, a new cell site's expected traffic can be estimated from the k most similar existing sites (population, area type, band, nearby sites).

misunderstandings: k-NN has no training, so it has no hyperparameters.
k, the distance metric, weighting and scaling are all choices to tune.
A bigger k is always safer.
Too big a k ignores local structure and favours the majority class.
It matters hugely: distances are dominated by large-range features.
Tuning on the test set is fine if you're careful.
Any tuning on the test set makes its score optimistic. Use validation or cross-validation.
takeaways: Instance-based (lazy) learners store data and compare at query time.
k-NN votes (classes) or averages (numbers) over the k closest points.
Distance choice matters: Minkowski family, matching/Jaccard for categories, Gower for mixed data, and always scale.
Choose k by validation (elbow), weight closer neighbours, and use locally weighted regression for smooth curves.
Select models with validation or k-fold cross-validation; keep the test set for the final estimate.
thirty: Instance-based learning keeps the training examples and predicts by comparing a new case with the most similar ones. k-nearest neighbours votes among the k closest points for a class, or averages them for a number. Similarity depends on the distance: Euclidean, Manhattan or supremum for numbers, mismatch or Jaccard for categories, Gower for mixed data, with features scaled first. Choose k with validation, weight closer neighbours more, and use locally weighted regression for curved targets. Always tune on validation folds and use the test set only once.

check.q: k-NN is called a lazy learner because…
opts: It defers work until prediction time
check.why: Little training, more work per prediction.

check.q: For a numeric target, k-NN predicts…
opts: The mean (or median) of the k neighbours

check.q: Income ranges 20,000–200,000 and age 20–60. Without scaling, distances are dominated by…
Why not choose k using the test set?
check.why: The test set must stay unseen.
